Did you ask him where Dr. Bosanac was, as well as some other staff?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: According my knowledge, not -- we went there only for this particular case. And it was up the head of mission how, and -- and our headquarters in Zagreb, how and which way we will proceed the problem. So we were sent there only to -- to speak about -- about those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to have this document tendered as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number 332.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: During examination-in-chief you said that the mission notified some European countries related to the taking away of the POWs. Can you tell us how that was done, via what channels; but first and foremost, do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on the spot, so it was -- it was on -- on leaders of the -- of the mission, and what I remember is that Ambassador Perrin was asking immediately to -- to have a contact with Dr. Bosanac and he got it -- the permission, I think, after 15 days or something like that, I -- I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Perrin tell you what the results of the effort undertaken through the European Community and certain of its instances, and concerning the attempts to find out about the fate of the POWs from the General Staff of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please see 0D00-0242 in the original. The English version is 0D00-0244. This is another report of the Monitoring Commission overseeing the activities of the ECMM, the date being the 22nd of November, 1991, concerning the period from the 21st, because, as I believe the ECMM did not send the report on that day, but rather there was a report that dealt with the 21st and the 22nd together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting my learned friend. On the transcript I don't have any reply to the question that was posed at 17.29.58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasic, you might clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to thank my learned friend. I failed to notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, could you please take a look at the screen, page 46, lines 17 to 20. The question was: "What were the results of the activities undertaken by the Monitoring Mission through the European Community and the JNA top staff?" What were the results, in your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know, that the case of -- of this alleged man was -- or has disappeared in -- in -- so it -- there were no complaints afterwards, but I am not really aware about the situation. So it -- it was the main -- the main purpose of the meeting, why we were asked to come to headquarters. And I -- I cannot refer more about this document, because I can see only preamble of the document, and not the -- the subject, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, I believe we have misunderstood each other. I wanted to deal with this document, but we omitted an answer in the transcript. I wanted to clarify that first. My question was, do you have any knowledge as to whether, after the information sent to the bodies of the European Community and some of the states, as well as to the top staff of the JNA, were there any results, that is whether the POWs taken away from the Vukovar Hospital were found and whether it resulted in a -- in an ability to find Dr. Bosanac and some of the staff of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... one of those papers there is -- there is a report about a meeting with Dr. Bosanac and there are mentioned some prisoners of war, or -- or I am not quite sure if it is this paper. So there is -- there is mentioned that there are -- there is 30 -- all personnel or prisoners of war, I'm not sure. So there is certain document which has mentioned that, but according my knowledge, I can't say anything, because it is not any more in my memory. So I -- I can't say if there is any effect or -- and which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To go back to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have some seven to ten questions left. Would this be a good time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was hanging on, waiting for you to reach your last question, Mr. Vasic. You might look closely at the [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I just deal with two administrative matters? I can deal with it now, or I can deal with it after my friend Mr. Vasic has concluded. The first relates to Dr. Bosanac, who has now arrived in The Hague. She's been recalled in relation to a document that was presented to OTP when she came -- or we went to Vukovar in September. That is the first part. We make no application to speak to her or proof her in relation to that document. There are, however -- there is a document which was disclosed after she had concluded her evidence, which the Defence wished to ask some questions of her in relation to that. As, indeed, there is Dr. Njavro, who must conclude his cross-examination from Mr. Sljivancanin and re-examination. May I deal with the Dr. Bosanac point? And it is this: Because it strikes into two other witnesses. Would the Court object if the Prosecution are -- the Prosecution speak to any of the witnesses - and I take Dr. Bosanac by way of example - prior to her coming in to giving evidence only on the document which she was never ever spoken to about, or does the Court wish us to provide the document to her, for the Prosecution not to speak to her in any way, and for her just to be cross-examined on document and that alone? And I seek the Court's guidance in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can it be clarified, is this a document which you discovered and disclosed after her evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's correct. And it applies to two other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do any Defence counsel wish to speak in respect of that? Mr. Vasic, Mr. Borovic, Mr. Lukic? Mr. Lukic is standing. He is a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But a few words, Your Honour. We have been asked by the OTP as to our position relating to this topic. Our position will be that we will rely on what will be put forward by the Chamber pertaining to the documents disclosed under Rule 68. If we were to go into detail we would have to ask for some additional information from the OTP as to when they took possession of those documents, whether they had those documents when they were proofing their witness; but in any case, we will go with the Chamber's decision. And this pertains exclusively to those witnesses who had concluded their evidence but are now being recalled. And Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence will use its right of discretion to examine the one witness that is important for us, and we are of the position that the OTP should and must not be allowed to communicate with him regarding the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you putting there that in respect of the one witness who is still the subject of cross-examination, that you would object to any discussion? Is that the point you're making?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Njavro. We haven't even begun examining him and we believe that the OTP shouldn't be allowed to communicate with him at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the Chamber would allow the Prosecution to speak to a witness who is recalled in the circumstances we're dealing with but only regarding the fresh document, but would indicate an exception in the case of Dr. Njavro. If you want an opportunity to speak to Dr. Njavro, you must seek that after the conclusion of cross-examination and before your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's very helpful. May I deal with the second point? It's quite simply this, and it is -- it may come as some surprise to the Court, but with regard to Ambassador Kypr, that was -- there are a number of documents, and it took quite a lengthy period of time in chief. Those documents still exist and Dr. Schou is the next witness. What we are trying to do is minimise all the documentation for Dr. Schou. Much of it is duplicated but there are some other original documents. He is here, we are trying to, as I say, refine the list. And I wonder, bearing in mind that I suspect the cross-examination of Ambassador Kypr will go well into the day tomorrow, whether Dr. Schou could commence on Thursday morning immediately? Even if it does mean a slightly shorter day tomorrow, because we can save a lot of time by dealing with those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be convenient, especially encouraged by the thought that it could save the very great deal of time that was unfortunately taken as we dealt with the documents with the present witness. Something is getting feedback from somewhere, I'm not sure from where. I see the culprit, he's turned off the microphone. Very well. There's still a bit of echo, but not as bad. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were they the only two points?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Based on your directions, I no longer wish to put questions to the witness regarding -- regarding the document that was on the screen. Could we now instead see 0D05 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you mean to tender that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The one that is on the screen, we didn't even deal with it. And for the reasons of efficiency and economy, I will move on to another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have an adjournment, and other things, counsel have a different understanding of what has happened. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The number is 0D05-01 -- no, 0060, in the original. And 0D05-063 [as interpreted] in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: For you, Mr. Kypr, that's tab 27. Thank you. Sir, I believe you've already found that document in your collection. As far as I can see, this is a report on the evacuation of the hospital in Vukovar, dated 21st and 22nd of November, put together by Mr. Cunningham, I believe.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the first page is -- has an authority signature Cunningham. And in the text there are probably remarks of Colonel Cunningham as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe my colleagues will deal with this topic in more detail, but I'm interested in only two things regarding that. Perhaps we could now look at page 00381349, that's the second comment, item 2, states: "EC monitors should not be prohibited from participating in any activity, no matter what the phase of the activity and either before or after the activity. And such activities should include only those that demand their monitoring. During the evacuation in Vukovar, we were forbidden to meet with the hospital management the evening before evacuation, based on the orders of Admiral Brovet, and through our JNA liaison officer." That's what the report states?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... written in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another thing that interests me in this document is to be found on page 00381428 concerning the convoy. This is item 5: "At approximately 06.45 hours, Schou and Kypr departed SM --" that is Sremska Mitrovica -- "for Vukovar to obtain the remaining patients. This part of the evacuation is covered by Kypr's report. Loading of the wounded from SM started at approximately 0810 and it was completed by 1100. Of note, the JNA assisted from senior captains to the lowest enlisted rank. Despite very hazardous slippery conditions, no patient was caused additional injury through poor handling. The convoy departed approximately at 11.15 and arrived at the meeting point at 12.22. No convoy on the Croat side in sight. As well, the handover point was located in a very poor place as the road was narrow with no manoeuvreing room. As a result, it was decided to move the handover location to Dvorovi, some distance down the road where there was sufficient room to manoeuvre." Sir, is this what this item states?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is written originally in English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to read another passage from the document to be found among the several final sentences of this paragraph, that is item 5. "At the conclusion of the handover, the people attending the meeting were one Croatian doctor, Colonel Pavkovic, a senior monitor from Zagreb, and myself to confirm that all dealings with the wounded had been carried out in a professional manner. All parties, especially the Croat medical personnel, agreed that the wounded had been accorded every consideration possible." Mr. Kypr, were you able to locate this portion?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is written there. Sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may suggest to have this document tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit Number 333, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have another document on the screen, 0D05-0100 in the original, and its B/C/S translation, 0D05-0106.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, this is report QV-18. I don't think it's in the binder forwarded by our learned colleague, therefore, I don't believe it's in any of the tabs that we have. With the assistance of the usher, I can provide a hard copy for you. It will probably be easier for you to read than reading from the screen. Thank you. Sir, this is a report on the activities of the Monitoring Mission on the 27th, that is on the 24th of November, 1991. First of all, were you personally involved in this visit to Vukovar on the 24th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the date is the 27th, but I cannot guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Were you in Vukovar on the 27th? I believe this document concerns the 27th.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if I were in -- in -- in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the title the date of the 27th of November is mentioned. I wanted to draw your attention to item 1. It says, "Situation in Vukovar. As previous report, the 24th of November." Does that mean that there was another report about the 24th of November as to the activities of the Monitoring Mission in Vukovar? Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please turn to page 00381448. (A) of the report states: "Dr. Ivankovic doesn't know anything about what's happening with the hospital. 'I have nothing to do with that.' I don't know anything about the bodies around the hospital. As for Dr. Bosanac, he said that she had made an ideological hospital and created a fortress out of it. From the roof there was firing at planes and also mortars were fired. Our team was not able to find any evidence of that on the roof. He doesn't know how many people were arrested in the course of the evacuation. According to the doctor, there were about 100 to 150 members of the National Guard." Can you please confirm that this is written in this part of the report.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is written in the text of report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kypr. I would also like to draw your attention to another part, which is on the next page, 00381449, and it refers to Luzac. It states: "The village was not as destroyed as Vukovar. There are a few houses that have been hit, but not destroyed because they were only hit with light weapons. We had contact with Captain Dragomir Lalic, the commander of the Territorial Defence. He told us that about 500 out of a total of 1.000 inhabitants have already returned." Mr. Kypr, is this what it says in this report?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender -- again, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is written in the original text of the copy I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this document as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number 334.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, you told us that you were in charge of monitoring the media, the news programmes which were broadcast, both in Serbia and in Croatia at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible only for Serb TV, because we cannot see Croatian TV in -- in our places.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you read the Croatian press at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some pieces, if it was possible. If we got them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know if you were aware that shortly before the fall of Vukovar - so in late November, 1991 - the media published a news item about children that were killed in a Vukovar kindergarten, about a necklace made by a member of the HDZ made out of children's fingers. Are you aware of such items that were published in the media?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that it was on -- in Serb media, but I cannot precisely say if it was on TV or in the press. And, to be precise, I cannot follow each day TV, because you can see that sometimes there were negotiations or other tasks even in the evening, so it was not possible to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, can you please tell me if you possibly heard from the Croatian media about a Croatian government meeting of the 17th of November, 1999 [as interpreted] when it was discussed whether Marin Vidic's request should be granted to negotiate with Goran Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me if, during your stay in Zagreb, you learned about the arrest of the Labrador Group. It was an intelligence group.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And my last question: Did you ever discuss with the other European observers' team about the problems that the turning back of the convoy had near Lipovac and then the firing at the convoy near Nustar, what problems that created as far as the organisation was concerned. The convoys were forced to move around in that area, and then finally they reached Bosnia, and later Croatia through Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please repeat your answer. Mr. Kypr, thank you for your answers, and I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. We'll just wait a little bit. Your Honours, we're also getting used to the new courtroom. It's our first day, it's not so easy, but we'll manage.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kypr. I am Mira Tapuskovic, I am one of the Defence attorneys for Mr. Radic. And in the time that we have left until 7.00, I'm going to be asking you a number of questions. During the examination-in-chief, and in response to questions by my learned friend Mr. Vasic, you provided an explanation several times about what your mandate was. So, to repeat, your mandate, or your tasks were delineated in the memorandum of understanding which was signed after the Brioni Agreement.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your assignments at the time were to observe the developments in the field, and you had the option of communicating with both sides or with a number of sides in the conflict. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was also your task to mediate, in a way, between the sides to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As part of that assignment did you also believe that it was your duty or obligation to submit reports on possible violations of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask you, ma'am, which agreement do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The memorandum of understanding is what I was thinking of.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. Because it was the case where -- when, for instance, JNA was complaining that one of our monitors committed -- or violated the -- the rules, so we received this message, and we reacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were questioned in the Dokmanovic case, you said that one of your tasks was to provide conditions for convoys, meaning not only the convoy that was going from Vukovar, but convoys in general that were being planned at that time, also from the territory of Croatia. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were the only impartial body which was respected from both sides. So using this trust from both sides, we were asked to -- to cover those convoys with -- with our presence, to -- to improve the common trust, let's say, or to assist.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that you could carry out this task that you were given, you had to cooperate very closely in the field with the International Committee of the Red Cross, right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes or not. Because there are two things: One is that rules of International Red Cross, Geneva Conventions, it belongs to very old, very valid system of humanitarian aid and help and on -- on the front line, in prisons, and so on and so on. So it's -- their task is much, much wider than ours and covers almost all humanitarian questions. We were very limited, and I have guide-lines for monitors that -- that this part of the business should be handover or run by -- by International Red Cross because they have more personnel, and they're equipped by the law and by -- by even respect from -- from sides. European Union mission was very new at that time in the territory and had a very limited mandate.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you answer my question whether you communicated in the field as well as in other areas, or did you have any kind of formal contacts with the International Committee of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: According formal contacts, I don't remember. But it happens because formal contacts are usually on the top of the mission. So it was done, and I remember some documents which are relating to that, that it was done in Zagreb, from our headquarters in Zagreb there was the official contact. We were cooperating with International Red Cross, or we have met with -- with representatives in -- I remember during some meetings. One of them was the 18th or 19th of November in Negoslavci. But still, and you can see in Colonel Cunningham's remarks that they insisted to do their job, and it is understandable, alone. It is understandable because their rules are another than ours, and the incompatibility of tasks and rules is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. I would now like you to turn to tab 27, please, and to go to page 00381429, and that's page 2 out of total of 3 pages. We have comments there, and messages, or lessons learned. And then in item 1 I'm going to read to you the following: "[In English] If the ICRC is to be involved in any associated activity with the EC monitors, then their part must be completed as agreed." [Interpretation] In parentheses, it says: "(Paragraph 6 of the fax message referred.)" Mr. Kypr, and I'm concluding it correctly, I hope, if I say that based on this paragraph you can see that it was indispensable to have joint activities, or linked activities by the International Committee of the Red Cross and European Community observers in the field, if I understand that correctly.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And we insisted a few times, I remember, that -- that we wished to have a cooperation with this ICRC. And -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you then, please, tell us, because you said that there were some contacts, and that this was an organisation that we are very familiar with. How many staff did the International Committee of the Red Cross have in the area covered by the observer mission, especially in the area covered by the regional centre from Belgrade that were you a part of?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and really I -- I -- I am convinced that I haven't got such an information. I remember one remark concerning four Red Cross cars in -- in some Cunningham's report, but I -- I can't tell because it was their job.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I was asking you about the number of staff, not the level of their equipment, but if you don't know, then that's fine. Yesterday - and this is reference for my colleagues; page 6.643 - you said that the task of the International Committee of the Red Cross was to go to the hospital to draft a list of the patients and to draw up an evacuation scheme or plan. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember the -- it was not report, but guide-lines coming from Zagreb to Belgrade where it is mentioned that they will be in -- in the hospital at 8.00 p.m. and that they will provide us with a list of -- of people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more about the instruction that the regional centre from Belgrade received from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... find it in few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kypr, could you please repeat your answer, because it was not registered in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this -- those guide-lines came from Zagreb and it's a part of -- of the documentation, I believe so. So we can go through and we can find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary. We just need to bring this paper part to the smallest degree possible. What I would like to know is that when you were in the regional centre in Belgrade, were you informed about the activities that the International Committee of the Red Cross was supposed to implement out in the field? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told, there is -- there is this information somewhere in the documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kypr, I would now like you to look at tab 25. This is a document, Vukovar 9 - this is so that my colleagues can keep track of where we are - and that's Exhibit 321. If I remember correctly, yesterday you said that this document was most probably drafted in the Zagreb centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just to be sure, these are pages 00381417.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... first page of report.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. This report was most probably drafted on the basis of the reports of the teams and the regional centres. Is my conclusion correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say what are all those resources. I believe that the main part of resources comes from regional centres or from monitoring teams, but there can be even -- even other meetings of -- of -- in headquarters, and so on, so I cannot testify what is the source of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at page 2 out of a total of 8 pages of this document, and that's English ERN number 00381418. Have you found it? At the top of the page, it says, "Team reports." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After that, we have item 7.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "[In English] Teams from Zagreb and Belgrade supported from Sarajevo were all heavily involved in the convoys and their reports are as follows." [Interpretation] This item 7, as an introduction, does that confirm that this report was compiled on the basis of team reports from Zagreb, Belgrade and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am sure that at least the first part is -- is based on -- on reports of teams. Conclusions, observations can be done even in Zagreb, I -- I don't know the -- the author of that. But it can come even -- even from -- from reports of monitors.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kypr. I would kindly ask you to go to page 2 of 8 in the same document. The number of the English text is ERN 00381418. 418. There is paragraph 7, let us now move to the next page, 419, subitem (b). It states, "Teams Belgrade/Sarajevo." That's page 3 of 8. (ii), that is a second item under subitem (b), reads the following: "[In English] Loading of the sick, wounded, and staff took until 1430 hours and was described as disorganised and chaotic, with no visible action by the ICRC apart from arguments with the military representatives." [Interpretation] Is this what is stated in this item?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is written on there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that this was the opinion of two teams, that of Belgrade and that of Sarajevo, stating that there was no visible action on the part of the International Committee of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that -- you have mentioned -- you have mentioned Sarajevo. And I don't think that team from Sarajevo was in -- in Vukovar's hospital, so they cannot comment that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please go one item above the one I read out. I read out (ii), and then we have (i), and then a heading, subitem (b), it says, "Teams Belgrade/Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the first paragraph speak about two teams went to Vukovar. It depends -- I don't know which -- which teams it were, because it -- maybe it is because the team was splitted afterwards, so I -- I don't know. I -- I don't remember other team, but in those circumstances ...

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Could we now move to page 6 of 8 in this document. ERN number 00381422. Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the top of the page the heading is, "Observations." Below it begins with item 9, and then we have subparagraphs (a) through (g), and could we please look at (g) itself. "[In English] The absence of any focal point of the ICRC."

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is written in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I don't mean to rush with my questions, but could you please explain something. This is a joint report. What does it mean, then, when it says, "The absence of any focal point for overall control of the ICRC"?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what does it mean, I can only speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go back to page 7 of 8 -- no, I believe this was that. Let's go to page 6 of 8, so that we could conclude with this document before we adjourn for today. ERN 00381422. First we have "Observations." Did you find that, Mr. Kypr?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will read item 8. "[In English] All teams involved in this exercise, including the tasking cell Zagreb, produced similar lists of observations as follows." [Interpretation] Is that what the document states?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is written there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us go down to subparagraph (e). You mentioned this paragraph yesterday on page 6643, for my learned friends. I will read out aloud again the subparagraph. "[In English] The ICRC must honour their role, in accordance with any agreement, for humanitarian convoys and not become agitated and aggressive at the first sign of trouble." [Interpretation] You said yesterday that the representative of the ICRC behaved aggressively. Would you doubt what is stated in subparagraph (e), having in mind that this was something that several teams in the field observed, as stated in item 8 at the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there was another argument or any other case which can be presented like something like that. So I -- I cannot say that this is the observation of other teams, because I -- I don't know if other teams were involved in moments where -- where Red Cross was there. So I cannot confirm that or deny that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's past 7.00 p.m., and I believe it is a good time for adjournment, and I believe we resume tomorrow in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, it is tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 29th day of March, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
